kurz: Why a great company and a great investment are two different things, and where the line between them runs.

bloecke.md:
## Quality as a measurable quantity

In this strategy, quality is a property of the balance sheet. Whether a company is likeable or makes a well-known product plays no role here. A quality company persistently earns more on the capital it employs than this capital costs. The yardstick is the [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|weighted average cost of capital (WACC)]]. The 2025 KPMG cost of capital study (around 300 mainly German companies, including 65% of the DAX 40 constituents) reports an average WACC of 8.5% and a cost of equity of 9.7%. There are considerable differences between industries. Technology and industrials are at 9.4%, automotive at 9.0%, real estate at 7.0%, and energy and raw materials at 6.3%.

There is therefore no absolute quality threshold. A return on capital of 8% means value creation for a property holding company and value destruction for an automotive supplier. The value created is measured by residual income. It results from the gap between [[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|return on invested capital (ROIC)]] and WACC, multiplied by the capital tied up.

bloecke.erklaerung: Without new debt and without new shares, a company can only grow as fast as it earns capital and puts it back to work. The compounder idea rests on this equation. Value arises from the product of a high return on capital and the amount of capital that can be invested at this return. The high return alone is not enough.

bloecke.md: Besides the return on capital, capital intensity matters. It indicates how much in fixed and current assets has to be tied up to generate one euro of revenue. The incremental return on capital is more informative here than the average return on total capital. This means the change in operating profit over a period, divided by the capital additionally tied up in the same period. This ratio shows what the most recently invested euro has earned, rather than what the investments of past decades yield.

Blue Chip Stamps, which Buffett and Munger controlled at the time and later merged into Berkshire, bought the confectioner in 1972 for $25 million. At that time, it had revenue of $30 million and pre-tax profit of just under $5 million, tying up $8 million of capital to do so, which corresponded to a pre-tax return of around 60% on the capital employed. In 2007, revenue was $383 million and pre-tax profit $82 million, with capital tied up of $40 million.

Over the 35 years, revenue grew by around 7.5% a year and pre-tax profit by just over 8%. That is rather moderate growth. However, around $77 million of additional annual profit required only $32 million of additional capital. By 2014, the business had generated a cumulative total of around $1.9 billion before tax.

See's is therefore a cash machine and not a compounder. The business could not itself absorb the billions it earned; they had to be invested elsewhere. Shareholders of such companies therefore also depend on management's capital allocation.

## Durable competitive advantages

High returns on capital only persist if something slows down competition. Two features of an [[Economic moat|economic moat]] can be verified in the financial statements without having to take a story on trust.

**Pricing power** shows in what happens to the gross margin when costs surge. Companies that can pass on higher raw material, energy and wage costs keep their gross margin roughly stable through an inflation surge. For the others, it collapses and only recovers years later. The years 2021 to 2023 provide a natural experiment for this, which can be traced in every annual report.

The second feature is **repeat purchases**. They show up in the revenue structure, for example in consumables for a durable device, in maintenance and subscription contracts or in everyday goods. Such revenue does not have to be won anew every year, requires less selling effort per euro and falls less in a downturn. The drawback is that the market knows about this stability and pays for it in the share price.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula follows from the present value of a stream of payments that grows forever at g. Of the profit, only the share (1 − g/ROIC) remains as free cash flow; the rest finances growth. The equation only applies to a steady state with g smaller than r. Growth of 15% must not be extrapolated forever in it.
bloecke.beispiel: With r = 9% and g = 6%, a ROIC of 25% gives a fair P/E of 25.3, a ROIC of 15% gives 20.0, a ROIC of 9% gives 11.1 and a ROIC of 7% only 4.8. If ROIC equals the cost of capital, g cancels out and the fair P/E is exactly 1/r. Growth without a return advantage creates no value.

bloecke.md: High returns on capital therefore justify high multiples mathematically. But that is only part of the calculation. Shareholder return is made up of earnings growth, the dividend and buyback yield, and the change in the multiple. Over one year, it is mainly the third component that determines the result; over ten years, it is the first. The third component does not disappear, however; it is merely spread over more years. If the multiple falls from 40 to 20 over ten years, it declines by 6.7% a year, because 0.5 to the power of 0.1 is 0.933. Since this factor is multiplied by the growth factor of earnings, at 12% earnings growth this costs 7.5 percentage points of return a year (1.12 × 0.933 = 1.045).

bloecke.md:
Around 1972, some 50 American blue chips were regarded as shares that you buy and never sell again, including Coca-Cola, McDonald's, IBM, Xerox, Polaroid, Avon and Disney. At the end of 1972, they traded at an average price-earnings ratio of around 42, individual shares such as Polaroid at well over 50, while the long-term market average was 15 to 20. In the 1973/74 bear market, they fell well behind the market. Jeremy Siegel later recalculated the group's performance up to 1998. According to his figures, an equally weighted portfolio of all the shares, bought at the peak in December 1972, performed almost in line with the S&P 500 over the following 26 years or so. By his calculation, shares that traded persistently above a P/E of 50, on the other hand, lagged the S&P 500 with few exceptions.

Most of the companies had not been badly chosen. Many of them still exist today and are highly profitable. Where returns were weak, this was mostly due to the excessive price. Some shares, however, also failed because of the business; Polaroid filed for creditor protection under Chapter 11 in 2001.

## Valuation risk in quality shares

Every valuation of a quality company rests on the rarely stated assumption that the high return on capital will be maintained. Economically, that is the unlikely case. Returns far above the cost of capital attract capital from competitors and imitators and bring regulators onto the scene. Normally, they therefore converge towards the average. A high historical return on capital proves that an advantage existed, but not that it will last.

If you pay 40 instead of 20 for one euro of profit, you are therefore buying, besides higher growth, above all its duration. The sensitivity is asymmetric. If growth flattens earlier than expected, a highly valued share is hit twice: once through the lower earnings base and once through the multiple, which falls with expectations. The two effects multiply. Practically all major losses in quality portfolios can be traced back to this relationship. Even merely mediocre news about the business can trigger them.

bloecke.md:
With RMW (Robust Minus Weak), Kenneth French publishes a long-short series that sets highly profitable companies against companies with low profitability. From July 1963 to July 2026, it returns a geometric mean of 2.81% a year with 7.9% volatility and a t-value of 3.10. After CMA, that is the lowest volatility of all standard factors, and 68% of calendar years were positive. For their measure Quality Minus Junk, which combines profitability, growth and safety, Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen find significant risk-adjusted returns in the US and in a global sample of 24 countries including the US. Feng, Giglio and Xiu show that most newly proposed factors are redundant, but that profitability passes this test.

Three limitations apply to the series. It is a long-short spread before costs, taxes and borrowing fees, not a portfolio result. It measures a ratio and makes no judgement on whether an advantage is durable. In addition, it too falls: from the end of 2024 to July 2026 by just over 15%. Investors in Germany who do not want to select quality shares themselves can find ETFs on quality indices. These buy according to the ratio and have higher ongoing charges than a standard world ETF, which currently costs 0.05% to 0.20% depending on the provider.

If a company reinvests its profit internally at a high return, this profit, after corporate taxes, continues to earn a return without any tax being incurred by the shareholder. If the same profit is distributed, 26.375% tax is due immediately: 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, excluding church tax.

Illustrative calculation over 20 years with €10,000 invested and a total return of 8%, without the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag):

- With internal compounding and a sale at the end, the capital grows to 10,000 × 1.08^20 = €46,610. Of the gain of €36,610, €26,954 remains after tax, so final wealth is €36,954. That corresponds to an effective 6.75% a year after tax.
- With full annual distribution, immediate taxation and reinvestment, 8 × 0.73625 = 5.89% remains net. Final wealth is €31,412.

The difference of around €5,500 arises without any additional return, solely from the timing of the tax. With funds and ETFs, this advantage is smaller because tax is due every year on the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale). At the base interest rate (Basiszins) of 3.20% for 2026, that is around €41 of tax per €10,000 of fund value at the start of the year.

A premium for quality is justified as long as the return on capital stays above the cost of capital and retained earnings can be deployed within the company at this return. If either condition falls away, a high P/E loses its foundation. The multiple then falls faster than the business deteriorates.

mitnehmen: Quality can be measured as the gap between the return on capital and the cost of capital; in Germany, the average WACC is around 8.5%, ranging between 6.3% and 9.4% depending on the industry.

According to g = ROIC × reinvestment rate, a compounder only arises from a high return combined with room for new capital; without this room, a high return produces a cash machine whose value depends on capital allocation.
Growth is value-neutral if ROIC equals the cost of capital and destroys value if it is below it; in the first case, the fair P/E is 1/r regardless of growth.

The entry price has an effect over the entire holding period, because a fall in the P/E from 40 to 20 over ten years costs 7.5 percentage points of return a year and turns 12% earnings growth into a 4.5% price return.

The Nifty Fifty of 1972 were mostly good companies at an average P/E of around 42 and performed almost in line with the market over the following 26 years or so, with the most expensive shares mostly below it; quality reduces business risk but does not protect against valuation risk.

begriffe.text: Company that can reinvest a large part of its profits in its own business at a return well above the cost of capital. It can be recognised by a high return on capital combined with a high reinvestment rate.

Change in operating profit divided by the capital additionally tied up in the same period. It measures what the most recently invested euro has earned, instead of the average of all earlier investments.
(ROIC − WACC) × invested capital. Only this part of profit lies above the cost of capital and creates value. The operating variant is called Economic Value Added.
Ability to pass cost increases on to customers without losing volume. It can be tested by looking at how the gross margin develops during inflationary periods.
Amount of fixed and current assets tied up per euro of revenue. With low capital intensity, growth needs little additional capital.
